children.translated_text: Om. Homage to the Buddha.
He who in every way has destroyed all darkness and has raised the world up from the mire of saṃsāra,
having bowed to him, I shall expound the treatise called the <s>Abhidharmakośa</s>, a śāstra concerning things as they really are.

children.text: prajñāmalā sānucarābhidharmaḥ tatprāptaye yāpi ca yacca śāstram
children.translated_text: Pure wisdom, together with its attendants, is Abhidharma; and so too is whatever treatise exists for attaining that.
Because its meaning enters here fully, and because this is its support, this work is called the <s>Abhidharmakośa</s>.

children.text: dharmāṇāṃ pravicayamantareṇa nāsti kleśānāṃ yata upaśāntaye'bhyupāyaḥ
children.translated_text: For without the discrimination of dharmas there is no means for the pacification of the afflictions.

children.text: kleśaiśca bhramati bhavārṇave'tra lokastaddhetorata uditaḥ kilaiṣa śāstrā ||
children.translated_text: And through the afflictions the world wanders here in the ocean of becoming; for that reason, indeed, this śāstra has been proclaimed.
Dharmas are contaminated and uncontaminated; conditioned dharmas, except for the path, are contaminated.
They are contaminated because the contaminants lie latent in them.
The truth of the path is uncontaminated, and the unconditioned is also threefold:

children.text: ākāśaṃ dvau nirodhau ca tatrākāśam anāvṛtiḥ ||
children.translated_text: space and the two cessations. Among these, space is non-obstruction.
Analytical cessation is disjunction, separately in each case.
The other cessation, through non-analytical cessation, is the absolute obstruction of arising.
Those conditioned dharmas, again, are the five aggregates beginning with form.
They alone are the three times, the bases of discourse, possessing issue, and possessing substance.
The contaminated aggregates are also the aggregates of appropriation.

children.text: duḥkhaṃ samudayo loko dṛṣṭisthānaṃ bhavaśca te ||
children.translated_text: They are suffering, origin, the world, the seat of views, and becoming.
Form is the five faculties, the five objects, and non-informative form as well.
The lucid material bases of the corresponding consciousnesses, beginning with the eye, are the eye and the other faculties.
Form is twofold and twentyfold; sound, however, is eightfold, taste is sixfold,
odor is fourfold, and the tangible has an elevenfold nature.
That continuity, wholesome or unwholesome, belonging even to one whose mind is distracted or absent,
and based on the great elements, is called non-informative form.
The elements are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element.
They are established by functions such as sustaining, and are hardness, moisture, heat, and motion.
In worldly convention, earth is called color and shape.
Water, fire, and wind are likewise elements, and yet also are so conventionally designated.
Those very faculties and objects are accepted as the ten bases and ten elements.
Feeling is experience; conception has the nature of grasping marks.
The other conditioned factors apart from the four are the aggregate of formations; and these three again,
together with non-informative form and the unconditioned, are called the dharma-base and the dharma-element.

children.text: vijñānaṃ prativijñaptiḥ mana āyatanaṃ ca tat
children.translated_text: Consciousness is awareness of an object; it is the mind-base.

children.text: dhātavaḥ sapta ca matāḥ ṣaḍ vijñānānyatho manaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Seven elements are recognized: the six consciousnesses and, further, mind.
The consciousness that has just passed immediately after the six is called mind.
For establishing the sixth support, eighteen elements are remembered.
The complete inclusion of all dharmas is by one aggregate, one base, and one element,
by intrinsic nature, because they are separated from the nature of another.
There is unity of an element because of commonality in kind, range, and consciousness.
Though the eyes and the rest are dual, twofold arising is for the sake of beauty.
The aggregates, bases, and elements mean heaps, doors of arising, and lineages.
Because of delusion, faculty, and preference in three kinds, there are the three teachings beginning with aggregates.
Because they are roots of dispute and causes of saṃsāra, and because of sequence,
feeling and conception are placed as separate aggregates apart from the mental factors.
The unconditioned is not stated among the aggregates because its meaning does not fit there; the sequence again
is according to coarseness, defilement, vessel, and so on, and according to the meaning of the elements.
The first five come first because their objects are present; the group of four follows because their objects are material.
The other is later because its operation is farther and quicker; or the sequence is according to their place.
For the purpose of specification, because of predominance, and because many foremost dharmas are included,
one base is called form and one is called dharma.
The eighty thousand dharma-aggregates that the Sage proclaimed
are either speech or name; thus they are included within form and formations.
Some say they are the measure of the śāstra. How is there one-by-one division of the aggregates and so on?
But a dharma-aggregate is described as an antidote to a disposition.
Likewise the other aggregates, bases, and elements too, according as appropriate,
are to be understood within the things already stated, after determining their own specific characteristics.
An aperture is called the space-element, and so, it is said, are light and darkness.
The consciousness-element is consciousness; contaminated dharmas are the supports of birth.
Here one thing, form, is visible; ten things, having form, are resistant.
Eight are morally indeterminate; those same, excluding form and sound, are without form and sound.
Three other elements belong to the desire-realm; in the form-realm all fourteen exist,
except for the odor, taste, nose-consciousness, and tongue-consciousness elements.
The elements belonging to the formless realm are mind, dharma, and mind-consciousness.
These three may be contaminated or uncontaminated; the remaining ones are contaminated.
The five consciousness-elements have initial and sustained thought.
The last three are of three kinds; the rest are devoid of both.
Because of conceptual construction as investigation and recollection, they are not without conceptuality.

children.text: tau prajñā mānasī vyagrā smṛtiḥ sarvaiva mānasī ||
children.translated_text: Those two are distracted mental wisdom and memory; memory is entirely mental.
Seven, the mind-elements, have an object, and half of the dharma-element also has one.

children.text: navānupāttās te cāṣṭau śabdaśca anye nava dvidhā ||
children.translated_text: Nine are unappropriated; those eight and sound are so; the other nine are twofold.

children.text: spraṣṭavyaṃ dvividhaṃ śeṣā rūpiṇo nava bhautikāḥ
children.translated_text: The tangible is twofold; the remaining nine material things are derived from the elements.
A part of the dharma-element is also accumulated; ten material things are accumulated.
The external tetrad of elements cuts and is cut.
It is burned and it weighs; in this way there is debate about what burns and what weighs.
The five internal ones are born of maturation and accumulation; that which is born of maturation is internal.
Sound is not resistant. Eight are unobstructed; they arise from outflow and from maturation.
Among the three kinds, one is substantially existent; the last three are momentary.

children.text: cakṣurvijñānadhātvoḥ syāt pṛthak lābhaḥ sahāpi ca ||
children.translated_text: For the eye and the consciousness-element there may be acquisition separately, and also together.
Leaving aside the twelve internal ones and the elements beginning with visible form, the one called the dharma-element remains.

children.text: sabhāgaḥ tatsabhāgāśca śeṣāḥ yo na svakarmakṛt ||
children.translated_text: They are either associated or associated with that; the rest are those which do not perform their own function.

children.text: daśa bhāvanayā heyāḥ pañca ca antyāstrayastridhā
children.translated_text: Ten are to be abandoned by cultivation; the last five and the three are threefold.
What is undefiled is not to be abandoned by seeing; neither is form, nor what is not produced from the sixth.
A portion of the eye and of the dharma-element is view, in eight ways.
The understanding that arises together with the five consciousnesses is not view, because it does not ascertain.

children.text: cakṣuḥ paśyati rūpāṇi sabhāgaṃ na tadāśritam
children.translated_text: The eye sees visible forms, when it is functioning; the consciousness resting on it does not.

children.text: vijñānaṃ dṛśyate rūpaṃ na kilāntaritaṃ yataḥ ||
children.translated_text: Visible form is seen, not, they say, when it is screened, because of an intervening obstruction.
One sees even with both eyes, because vision is distinct.
The eye, ear, and mind have objects not reached by them; the other three are otherwise.
It is held that with the three, smell and the rest, there is apprehension of an object equal to them.
For the last, its support is past; for the five, the support is simultaneous with them.
Because they are altered when that is altered, the supports are the eye and the rest.
Therefore, because they are not common, consciousness is designated by those supports.

children.text: na kāyasyādharaṃ cakṣuḥ ūrdhvaṃ rūpaṃ na cakṣuṣaḥ
children.translated_text: The eye is not lower than the body; visible form is not higher than the eye.

children.text: vijñānaṃ ca asya rūpaṃ tu kāyasyobhe ca sarvataḥ ||
children.translated_text: And its consciousness is the same; but visible form, and both of the body, may be in every case.

children.text: tathā śrotraṃ trayāṇāṃ tu sarvameva svabhūmikam
children.translated_text: So also the ear. For the three, however, everything is only of its own level.
Body-consciousness may be lower or of its own level; the mind is indeterminate.

children.text: pañca bāhyā dvivijñeyāḥ nityā dharmā asaṃskṛtāḥ
children.translated_text: Five external objects are known by two consciousnesses; unconditioned dharmas are eternal.
Half of the dharma-element is a faculty, and the twelve are remembered as internal.

children.text: abhidharmakośabhāṣye dhātunirdeśo nāma prathamaṃ kośasthānaṃ samāptamiti
children.translated_text: Thus in the <s>Abhidharmakośabhāṣya</s>, the first kośa-section, called the exposition of the elements, is completed.
In four purposes there is, it is said, predominance of five faculties, and in two purposes predominance of two.
There is predominance of four, of five, and of eight in defilement and purification.
Because of predominance in apprehending their own objects, and because of all this, the six faculties are so called.
Because of predominance over femininity and masculinity, the female and male faculties are distinguished from the body.
Because of predominance over the continuance of the group, defilement, and purification,
life, the five feelings, and faith and the rest are regarded as faculties.
The faculty called 'I shall know,' the faculty of knowledge, and likewise the faculty of one who has known,
are so called because of their predominance over successive attainment, beginning with nirvana.
The support of mind, its differentiation, its duration, defilement itself,
the equipment, and purification: to that extent there is what is called faculty.
Because of support, arising, duration, and experience in activity,
there are fourteen faculties; the others, alternatively, are faculties for cessation.

children.text: duḥkhendriyam aśātā yā kāyikī vedanā sukham
children.translated_text: The pain-faculty is the unpleasant bodily feeling; pleasure is pleasant bodily feeling.

children.text: śātā dhyāne tṛtīye tu caitasī sā sukhendriyam ||
children.translated_text: But in the third meditation it is mental, and that is the pleasure-faculty.

children.text: anyatra sā saumanasyaṃ aśātā caitasī punaḥ
children.translated_text: Elsewhere that mental pleasant feeling is satisfaction; unpleasant mental feeling, again,
is dissatisfaction. Equanimity is the middle feeling, both kinds, because it is without discrimination.
On the paths of seeing, cultivation, and training, there are nine, three, and three stainless faculties.

children.text: rūpīṇi jīvitaṃ duḥkhe sāsravāṇi dvidhā nava ||
children.translated_text: The material faculties, life, and pain are defiled; nine are of two kinds.
Life is karmic maturation; twelve are twofold, except for the last eight.
And except for dissatisfaction. One of these is such; ten have maturation, and two are twofold.
Mind, the other feelings, and faith and the rest, the group of eight, are wholesome in two ways.
Dissatisfaction, mind, and the other feelings are threefold; the rest are of one kind.
They belong to the desire-realm, except the stainless; they belong to the form-realm, except the female and male faculties,

children.text: duḥkhe ca hitvā ārūpyāptaṃ sukhe cāpohya rūpi ca ||
children.translated_text: and except pain; they belong to the formless realm, excluding pleasure and also what is material.
Mind and the three feelings are threefold; dejection is to be abandoned in two ways.

children.text: nava bhāvanayā pañca tvaheyānyapi na trayam ||
children.translated_text: Nine are to be abandoned by cultivation; five are also not to be abandoned, but not the three.
At the beginning in the desire-realms, two maturational faculties are obtained, but not by beings born spontaneously.

children.text: taiḥ ṣaḍ vā sapta vā aṣṭau vā ṣaḍ rūpeṣu ekamuttare ||
children.translated_text: By them six, or seven, or eight are obtained; in the form-realms six, and in the higher realm one.
At cessation through death, in the formless realm, life, mind,

children.text: upekṣāṃ caiva rūpe'ṣṭau kāme daśa navāṣṭau vā ||
children.translated_text: and equanimity cease; in the form-realm eight cease, and in the desire-realm ten, nine, or eight.

children.text: kramamṛtyau tu catvāri śubhe sarvatra pañca ca
children.translated_text: But in gradual death there are four, and in a good state everywhere five.
For the two final fruits there is acquisition of nine, and for two others by seven, eight, or nine.
Arhatship is said to be attained with eleven, since it is possible for one person.
One joined with equanimity, life, and mind is necessarily endowed with those three.
With pleasure and body he is endowed with four; one possessing eye and the rest is endowed with five.

children.text: saumanasyī ca duḥkhī tu saptabhiḥ strīndriyādimān ||
children.translated_text: One with satisfaction, and one with pain, is endowed with seven; one possessing the female faculty and the rest,
with eight. One endowed with the faculties of knowledge and of one who has known is endowed with eleven.
One furnished with the 'I shall know' faculty is endowed with thirteen.
With the fewest, a being lacking wholesome faculties is endowed with eight: feeling, mind, body, and life,
and so also an ordinary person in the formless realm, with equanimity, life, mind, and the wholesome faculties.
With the most, one is endowed with nineteen, excluding the stainless faculties.
A noble person with two sexes and passion is endowed with all except one sex and the two stainless faculties.
In the desire-realm an atom without sound consists of eight substances and is without faculty.
When it has the body-faculty it has nine substances; when it has another faculty it has ten substances.
Mind and mental factors are necessarily accompanied by all the marks of the conditioned,
or by acquisition. Mental factors are fivefold, according to the division into the great-ground and so on.

children.text: vedanā cetanā saṃjñā chandaḥ sparśo matiḥ smṛtiḥ
children.translated_text: Feeling, volition, perception, desire-to-act, contact, intelligence, mindfulness,
attention, resolve, and concentration are present in every mind.
Faith, carefulness, tranquility, equanimity, conscience, shame,

children.text: mūladvayamahiṃsā ca vīryaṃ ca kuśale sadā ||
children.translated_text: the two roots, non-harming, and energy are always present in the wholesome mind.
Delusion, heedlessness, laziness, lack of faith, torpor, and agitation;
and, in what is always afflicted and unwholesome, shamelessness and lack of embarrassment.
Anger, resentment, hypocrisy, envy, hostility, concealment, and avarice,
deceit, intoxication, and harmfulness belong to the class of minor defilements.
Because it has both initial and sustained thought, in a wholesome mind of the desire realm
there are twenty-two mental factors; remorse is additional in some cases.
In an isolated unwholesome mind, and in one joined with wrong view, there are twenty;
with four defilements, with anger and the rest, or with remorse, there are twenty-one.
In an obscured-neutral mind eighteen are taught; elsewhere, in an indeterminate mind, twelve.
Since sleep is not incompatible with any of them, wherever it occurs it is additional.
Remorse and sleep, being unwholesome, are therefore absent in the first dhyāna;
in the intermediate dhyāna there is initial thought, and beyond that sustained thought too is absent.
Shamelessness is disrespect toward what is blameworthy; lack of embarrassment is not seeing danger in it.

children.text: prema śraddhā gurutvaṃ hrīḥ te punaḥ kāmarūpayoḥ ||
children.translated_text: Faith is loving trust; shame is reverence. These again occur in the desire and form realms.
Initial thought and examination are respectively grossness and subtlety; pride is self-exaltation.

children.text: madaḥ svadharme raktasya paryādānaṃ tu cetasaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Intoxication is the complete taking-over of the mind of one attached to his own qualities.
Mind, thought, and consciousness have one meaning. Mind and mental factors
are associated in five ways: by basis, object, aspect, time, and so on.
The formations dissociated from mind are acquisition and non-acquisition, homogeneity,
the non-conscious state, the attainments, life, and the characteristics;
also the groups of names and the like. Acquisition is obtaining and possession.
Acquisition and non-acquisition apply to things fallen within one's own continuum and to cessations.
For things of the three times they are threefold; for wholesome and other things, wholesome and so forth.
For things belonging to one's own realm they belong to that realm; for things not so obtained they are fourfold.
For those in training and beyond training they are threefold; for what is not to be abandoned they are taught as twofold.
The acquisition of the indeterminate is innate, except for supernormal knowledge and magical creations.

children.text: nivṛtasya ca rūpasya kāme rūpasya nāgrajā
children.translated_text: So too of the obscured, and of form. In the desire realm, acquisition of form is not prior-born.
Non-afflicted indeterminate non-acquisition is threefold with regard to past and future things.
Non-acquisition is admitted for things belonging to the desire realm and so on, for stainless things, and for the path.
Common worldling status is lost through acquiring that state and by transition of level.
Homogeneity is the sameness of living beings. The non-conscious state occurs among the non-conscious gods.
It is the cessation of mind and mental factors, a result of maturation; they are the Bṛhatphala gods.
Likewise the non-conscious attainment occurs in the last dhyāna, from a wish for escape.
It is wholesome, experienced only upon rebirth, and not for a noble one; it is acquired in one temporal mode.
The so-called cessation attainment is similar, intended for abiding, and arises from the summit of existence.

children.text: śubhā dvivedyā'niyatā ca āryasya āpyā prayogataḥ ||
children.translated_text: It is wholesome, has two kinds of experience, is also indeterminate, belongs to a noble one, and is acquired through effort.
For the sage it is obtained with awakening, not before, because the thirty-four moments must be acquired.
The so-called cessation attainment has the desire and form realms as its basis; at first it arises among humans.
Lifespan, or life, is the support of warmth and consciousness.
The characteristics, again, are birth, aging, duration, and impermanence.
Birth-birth and the rest are theirs; those eight operate upon one dharma.
Birth is what produces the to-be-born, but not without causes and conditions.
Groups of names and the like are collections of designations, sentences, and syllables.
They are called sentient, belonging to the desire and form realms, outflow-born, and indeterminate.

children.text: sabhāgatā sā tu punarvipāko'pi āptayo dvidhā
children.translated_text: Homogeneity, however, is also maturation; acquisitions are twofold,
and the characteristics are outflow-born; attainments and possessions are likewise so classified.
Cause, coexistent cause, homogeneous cause, associated cause,
universal cause, and the cause called maturation: cause is accepted as sixfold.
The cause called cause is anything other than itself; coexistent causes are those that have mutual results,
like the elements, or like mind and the marks that follow mind and the marked object.

children.text: caittā dvau saṃvarau teṣāṃ cetaso lakṣaṇāni ca
children.translated_text: Mental factors, the two restraints, and their characteristics of mind
are followers of mind through time, result, goodness and so forth.
The homogeneous cause consists of similar things, earlier in their own class and level.
The path of the nine levels is reciprocal for what is equal or superior.
Those born from effort, such as what is made of hearing and reflection, are only of those same two kinds.
The associated cause consists of mind and mental factors sharing the same basis.
The cause called universal consists, among afflicted things, of prior universal factors in their own level.
The cause of maturation consists of unwholesome things and also wholesome things with outflows.
The universal and homogeneous causes operate over two times; three causes operate over three times.
The conditioned has fruits including separation; these do not belong to the unconditioned.
The fruit of maturation belongs to the last cause; the fruit of predominance belongs to the first.
For the homogeneous and universal causes there is outflow-result; for two causes there is the result of human effort.
Maturation is an indeterminate dharma, called sentient, arising from what is determinate.
An outflow-result resembles its cause; separation is destruction through insight.
Whatever arises by the power of something is its result born of human effort.
What is unprecedented belongs only to the conditioned; the conditioned is the fruit of the predominant cause.

children.text: varttamānāḥ phalaṃ pañca gṛ?hanti dvau prayacchataḥ
children.translated_text: Five present causes grasp a fruit, and two bestow it;
two, present and past, bestow it, while one past cause bestows it.
Afflicted things, maturation-born things, the remaining things, and the first noble states, respectively,

children.text: vipākaṃ sarvagaṃ hitvā tau sabhāgaṃ ca śeṣajāḥ ||
children.translated_text: arise excluding maturation, excluding the universal cause, excluding those two plus the homogeneous cause, and from the remaining causes.
Mind and mental factors, and likewise other things too, except for the associated cause,

children.text: catvāraḥ pratyayā uktāḥ hetvākhyaḥ pañca hetavaḥ ||
children.translated_text: have four conditions taught: the condition called cause consists of five causes.
Minds and mental factors that are not final, once arisen, are the immediately antecedent condition.
All dharmas are the object-condition; what is called cause is remembered as the predominant condition.

children.text: nirudhyamāne kāritraṃ dvau hetū kurutaḥ trayaḥ
children.translated_text: When ceasing, two causes perform their activity; three do so
when arising. The other two conditions operate contrariwise.
For the two attainments there are four causes, because they are accompanied by mental factors; for the other factors there are three.
Other things arise from two causes, but not from an Īśvara and the like, because of the ordered sequence and other reasons.

children.text: dvidhā bhūtāni taddhetuḥ bhautikasya tu pañcadhā
children.translated_text: The elements are twofold as causes of that; for what is derived from the elements, however, the cause is fivefold.
What is derived from the elements is threefold in relation to another such thing; for the elements themselves that relation is only onefold.
In the desire realm mind is wholesome or unwholesome, obscured or unobscured.
In the form and formless realms, apart from the unwholesome, it is so; the stainless mind is twofold.

children.text: kāme nava śubhāccittāccittāni aṣṭābhya eva tat
children.translated_text: In the desire realm, from a wholesome mind nine minds may follow; from exactly eight that wholesome mind may follow.
The unwholesome follows from ten; from it four arise. The obscured mind is likewise.
The unobscured mind follows from five; after it seven minds may immediately arise.
In the form realm, from a wholesome mind eleven minds arise; after nine minds that wholesome mind may arise.

children.text: aṣṭābhyo nivṛtaṃ tasmāt ṣaṭ tribhyo'nivṛtaṃ punaḥ
children.translated_text: The obscured mind follows from eight; from it six arise. Again the unobscured follows from three.

children.text: tasmāt ṣaḍ evāmārūpye tasya nītiḥ śubhātpunaḥ ||
children.translated_text: From it only six arise. In the formless realm the rule for that, again, is as follows from the wholesome mind.

children.text: nava cittāni tat ṣaṇṇāṃ nivṛtātsapta tattathā
children.translated_text: Nine minds arise; that mind follows from six. From the obscured, seven arise, and it too is the same.

children.text: caturbhyaḥ śaikṣam asmāttu pañca aśaikṣaṃ tu pañcakāt ||
children.translated_text: The learner's mind follows from four; from it five arise. The adept's mind, however, follows from five.
From it four minds arise. These twelve make twenty when divided in the three realms.
The wholesome is twofold: obtained through effort and obtained at rebirth.
In the desire realm the indeterminate is fourfold: maturation-born, deportment-related, craft-related, and magically created.
In the form realm it is the same, except for what is craft-related.

children.text: kliṣṭe traidhātuke lābhaḥ ṣaṇṇāṃ ṣaṇṇāṃ dvayoḥ śubhe
children.translated_text: With afflicted mind in the three realms there is acquisition of six, six, and two respectively; with wholesome mind,

children.text: trayāṇāṃ rūpaje śaikṣe caturṇāṃ tasya śeṣite ||
children.translated_text: there is acquisition of three in the form-born case, and of four in the learner's mind; in what remains of that,

children.text: abhidharmakośe indriyanirddeśo nāma dvitīyaṃ kośasthānaṃ samāptamiti ||
children.translated_text: the second kośasthāna of the <s>Abhidharmakośa</s>, called the exposition of the faculties, is complete.
Om. Homage to the <s>Buddha</s>.
The roots of existence are the six <s>anuśayas</s> (latent tendencies): attachment and hostility,

children.text: māno'vidyā ca dṛṣṭiśca vicikitsā ca te punaḥ ||
children.translated_text: conceit, ignorance, view, and doubt. Again, they are said to be seven,
because attachment is divided into six kinds; attachment to existence is born in two realms.
It is stated separately because it is inward-facing and in order to prevent the notion that it is liberation.
The views are five: personality view, false view, and extreme view,
and the views that cling to views and to rules and vows; thus, again, they become ten.
These ten are abandoned, respectively, as seven, seven, eight, and three, two, excluding certain views,
in the desire realm through seeing suffering and the other truths.
Four are to be abandoned by cultivation. The same, again without hostility,
apply in the form realm and likewise in the formless realm; thus they are held to be ninety-eight.
Those born at the summit of existence are destroyed by patience; the rest, to be abandoned by seeing,
are destroyed by seeing and cultivation, not by patience; those to be abandoned by cultivation are destroyed by cultivation alone.
The views concerning self, what belongs to self, permanence, annihilation, nonexistence, inferiority, and the corrupt remaining reading,
and the view concerning non-causality and the path: these are the five views.
With regard to Īśvara and the rest it proceeds from the inversion that there is an eternal self.
Therefore attachment to a cause is to be abandoned only by seeing suffering.
From three views comes the fourfold inversion, because of wrong reversal,
because of decisive misjudgment and superimposition; perception and mind occur under its influence.
There are seven conceits, ninefold; from three they are exhausted by seeing, by cultivation, and by patience.
Vexations such as killing and the rest are likewise to be abandoned by cultivation.
For the noble one there is no wish for nonexistence, nor do forms of harmful intent arise.
Nor is there the conceit 'I am,' because it is strengthened by view; nor is regret wholesome there.
The universal views are those to be abandoned by seeing suffering and its cause, and so too

children.text: vimatiḥ saha tābhiśca yā'vidyā've?ikī ca yā ||
children.translated_text: doubt together with them, and the ignorance associated with them, and the damaged separate form of ignorance.
Nine have an object in a higher level, excluding two views among these.
Except for acquisitions, the co-arisen factors that accompany them are also universal.
False view, doubt, the ignorance joined with those two, and then ignorance alone,
when to be abandoned by seeing cessation and the path, are six and have the stainless as their object.
The path that is cessation of one's own level belongs to six levels or to nine levels.
For those whose object it is, the path is their object, because paths are mutually causal.
There is no attachment to it, because it is to be rejected; there is no hatred, because it does no harm.
There is no conceit and no two kinds of clinging, because it is peaceful, pure, and supreme.
The universal latent tendencies lie latent in the whole of their own level,
because they take it as object; non-universal ones lie latent only in their own class.
They do not have the stainless or a higher level as object, because these are not appropriated and because they are opposed.

children.text: yena yaḥ samprayuktastu sa tasmin saṃprayogataḥ ||
children.translated_text: Whichever one is associated with something lies latent in it by association.
Above, all are indeterminate. In the desire realm, personality view,
extreme view, and delusion together with those two are so; the remaining ones here are unwholesome.
In the desire realm the roots of the unwholesome are attachment, hostility, and delusion.
The three unwholesome roots are craving, ignorance, and that cognition.
Since two operate above, the others say there are only four besides these.
They are craving, view, conceit, and delusion, because meditators have three, together with ignorance.
An answer may be categorical, analytical, by counter-question,
or to be set aside, as in questions about death and birth, the distinct self, difference, and the like.
With attachment, hostility, and conceit, when they are past or present,
one is bound to that object in which they have arisen and have not been abandoned.
Everywhere one is bound by future ones of these, by mental factors of one's own time, and by others,

children.text: ajaiḥ sarvatra śeṣaistu sarvaiḥ sarvatra saṃyutaḥ ||
children.translated_text: by unborn ones everywhere; with the remaining ones, by all of them everywhere one is bound.
Because existence in all times is stated, from the two, from an existent object, and from result,
and because that existence is affirmed, the <s>Sarvāstivādins</s> are accepted as fourfold.
They are named according to existence, characteristic, state, and otherness.
The third is best; the times are established by function.

children.text: kiṃ vighnaṃ tatkathaṃ nānyat adhvāyogaḥ tathā sataḥ
children.translated_text: What obstruction is there? How is that so, and why not otherwise? The connection with time belongs to what exists.
By what are things unborn and destroyed? The nature of dharmas is indeed profound.
When what is to be abandoned by seeing suffering has been abandoned, one is still connected with the remaining universal dispositions;
and when that prior class has been abandoned, with the remaining defilements that have that as their object.
Those born in the desire realm and to be abandoned by seeing suffering and cause and by cultivation
have as their object the undefiled consciousnesses obtained in their own three classes and in one form class.
Those born in the form realm have as their object the undefiled states of their own level, the three lower levels, and one higher level;
those born in the formless realm, because the three realms are reached, have the three vehicles and the stainless as their object.
All those to be abandoned by seeing cessation and the path have as their object what belongs to themselves and higher levels;
the stainless ones have as their object the last three of the three realms and the stainless.
The afflicted is twofold: with <s>anuśaya</s> (latent disposition) and not afflicted by latent dispositions;
from delusion and doubt comes wrong view, from that the view of a real personhood;
from that comes grasping at extremes, from that attachment to rules and observances, and then the views;
passion arises toward one's own view, pride also, and hatred toward another: this is the sequence.
From an unabandoned latent disposition, from an object that is present,
and from improper mental attention, a defilement has its complete cause.
In the desire realm, the defilements together with obsessions are the outflow of desire, except for
delusion; in the form and formless realms the latent dispositions themselves are the outflow of existence.
For they are indeterminate, inward-turned, and belong to concentrated levels;
therefore they are combined. Ignorance is the root, and so it is a separate outflow.
Likewise with floods and bonds; but the separate status of views is because of their sharpness.
Among the outflows, those without auxiliaries are not counted, since they are said not to be favorable to it.
The <s>upādāna</s>s (appropriations) are just as stated, together with ignorance, and twofold by the separation of views;

children.text: upādānāni avidyā tu grāhikā neti miśritā ||
children.translated_text: ignorance, however, is mixed in because it grasps, not because it is a view.
These eight follow along, and they lie latent in two ways;
and because they bind closely, they are remembered as <s>anuśaya</s>s.
They make one dwell, they flow out, they carry off, and they make things cohere;
they also appropriate: such are the etymologies of their names, beginning with <s>āsrava</s>.
Again, by the division into fetters and so on, they are taught as fivefold;
because of difference in substance, grasping, and generality, views form another fetter.
Because jealousy and avarice are wholly unwholesome, independent,
and both in that way, they are stated separately as a pair of fetters.
The lower-part fetters are fivefold: by two there is no passing beyond desire;
by three there is return again, since the three grasp the entrance and the root.
Desire for going, confusion about the path, and doubt about the path
are obstacles to liberation in its progress; therefore there is the threefold teaching.
The higher-part fetters are likewise five: the two passions belonging to the form and formless realms,
and agitation, pride, and delusion. Because of knowledge, the three bonds are taught.
Other afflicted mental factors that are called the aggregate of formations
are also secondary defilements because they arise from defilements, but they are not called defilements.
Shamelessness, lack of moral dread, jealousy, avarice, excitement,
remorse, torpor, and sleepiness are the eight obsessions.
Anger and concealment are born from passion, as are shamelessness, excitement, and avarice;
from concealment comes dispute; from ignorance come torpor, sleepiness, and lack of moral dread.
Remorse comes from doubt; rage and jealousy are connected with aversion;

children.text: anye ca ṣa?kleśamalāḥ māyā śāṭhyaṃ madastathā ||
children.translated_text: and there are six other stains of defilement: deceit, craftiness, intoxication,
hostility, rancor, and harmfulness. Among these, deceit and intoxication are born from passion,
while rancor and harmfulness are born from aversion.
Hostility comes from grasping at views, and craftiness arises from views.
Among them, shamelessness, lack of moral dread, torpor, sleepiness, and excitement are twofold.
The others are to be abandoned by cultivation; and the stains, likewise, are independent.
In the desire realm three are unwholesome, twofold; beyond that they are indeterminate.
Deceit and craftiness occur in desire and in the first dhyāna because of the deceiving of <s>Brahmā</s>;
torpor, excitement, and intoxication occur in the three realms; the others belong to the desire realm.
Those established in common with them and to be abandoned by seeing belong to the level of mental consciousness;
the independent secondary defilements have six consciousnesses as their basis, and the rest also do so.

children.text: sukhābhyāṃ saṃprayukto hi rāgaḥ dveṣo viparyayāt
children.translated_text: Passion is associated with the two pleasant feelings, while hatred is the opposite;
delusion is associated with all, and false view with mental unhappiness and happiness.
Doubt is associated with displeasure; the others born in desire are associated with satisfaction;
all are also associated with equanimity, each according to its own level, and so too those of higher levels.
Remorse, jealousy, anger, harmfulness,
rancor, and hostility are associated with displeasure, but avarice is the reverse.

children.text: māyā śāṭhyamatho mrakṣo middhaṃ cobhayathā madaḥ
children.translated_text: Deceit, craftiness, concealment, and sleepiness are both ways; intoxication too is both ways.
Equanimity is universal with the two pleasant feelings; the other four are associated with five feelings.
In the desire realm the hindrances are counted as five because they have one opposition, nutriment, and function;
they are two and five because of the obstruction of the aggregates and because of doubt.
Destruction occurs through fully knowing the object, through the destruction of that which has that object,
through abandoning the object, and through the arising of the counteragent.
The counteragent is fourfold, called the basis of abandonment, reality,
fault, and purification. A defilement is held to be abandoned because of its object.
Because of difference in characteristic, because of being opposed, and because of separation by place and time,
there is distance, as in the case of the two pairs: elements and morality, region and temporal path.
Their destruction occurs once; the acquisition of disconnection from them occurs again and again
when the counteragent arises, when the result is attained, and when the faculties are strengthened.
There are nine complete knowledges: the destruction of the two classes beginning with desire,

children.text: ekā dvayoḥ kṣaye dve te tathordhvaṃ tisra eva tāḥ ||
children.translated_text: one when two are destroyed, then two more, and above that exactly three.
The others are the destructions of the lower-part fetters, of form, and of all outflows.

children.text: tisraḥ parijñāḥ ṣaṭ kṣāntiphalaṃ jñānasya śeṣitāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Three complete knowledges are the fruit of the acquiescences; the remaining six belong to knowledge.
All are the fruit of the preparatory stage; alternatively, five are the fruit of the dhyānas.
There is one belonging to the preparatory stage, and one belonging to each of the three fundamental formless attainments.

children.text: āryamārgasya sarvāḥ dve laukikasya anvayasya ca
children.translated_text: All belong to the noble path; two belong to the worldly path and also to inferential knowledge.

children.text: dharmajñānasya tisrastu ṣaṭ tatpakṣasya pañca ca ||
children.translated_text: But three belong to knowledge of dharmas; six belong to that side, and five as well.
Because separation from the outflow-free is obtained, and because the summit of existence is made deficient,
because the two causes are uprooted, and because the elements are passed beyond, there is complete knowledge.
One who stands in the path of seeing is endowed with them, from not just one up to five.

children.text: bhāvanāsthaḥ punaḥ ṣa?ibharekayā vā dvayena vā ||
children.translated_text: One who stands in the path of cultivation, however, is endowed with six, or with one, or with two.
Their aggregation is due to dispassion toward a realm and to obtaining a fruit.

children.text: ekāṃ dve pañca ṣaṭ kaścijjahātyāpnoti pañca na ||
children.translated_text: A person abandons one, two, five, or six; he obtains five, but not the rest.
The discussion of complete knowledge is finished.
Thus, in the <s>Abhidharmakośa</s>, the fifth treasury-section, named the Exposition of the Latent Tendencies, is completed.
